title: Splints, Wounds & Catheters
body:
## Splint by injury

| Injury | Splint | Position | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Clavicle | Sling and swathe (or figure-of-eight) | Arm across the chest | Comfort over anatomy |
| Shoulder dislocation | Sling and swathe | Splint as found | Never force it into alignment |
| Humerus shaft | Sugar-tong (coaptation) plus sling | Elbow at `90` degrees | Watch the radial nerve — wrist drop |
| Elbow | Long-arm posterior | `90` degrees, forearm neutral | Brachial artery and median nerve checks |
| Forearm | Sugar-tong or long-arm posterior | Elbow `90`, wrist neutral | Immobilize elbow and wrist both |
| Distal radius (Colles) | Sugar-tong | Slight flexion and ulnar deviation | Recheck after reduction |
| Scaphoid / snuffbox tenderness | Thumb spica | Wrist slightly extended, thumb abducted as if holding a glass | Splint even with a normal X-ray |
| Hand / metacarpal | Ulnar gutter (`4th`/`5th`), radial gutter (`2nd`/`3rd`) | Position of function: wrist `20` degrees extended, MCP `70–90` flexed, IP near straight | Wrong position causes permanent stiffness |
| Finger | Buddy tape or foam-aluminum splint | Per injury | Pad between fingers |
| Femur, mid-shaft, closed, isolated | Traction splint | Leg extended, gentle traction | Contraindicated with pelvic fracture, hip or knee injury, or lower-leg/ankle/foot injury |
| Hip / pelvis | Vacuum mattress or scoop, pelvic binder at the greater trochanters | Supine, knees supported | Binder goes over the trochanters, not the iliac crests |
| Knee | Knee immobilizer or long-leg posterior | `10–20` degrees of flexion | Check for knee dislocation with popliteal artery injury |
| Tibia / fibula | Long-leg posterior plus stirrup | Ankle at `90` degrees | High compartment syndrome risk |
| Ankle | Posterior plus stirrup (sugar-tong) | Ankle neutral, `90` degrees | Do not let the foot droop |
| Foot / metatarsal | Short-leg posterior or hard-soled shoe | Ankle `90` degrees | |
| Spine | Cervical collar plus vacuum mattress or scoop | Neutral inline | Motion restriction, not rigid boarding |

Material notes: splint the joint above **and** below. Plaster is about `8–10` layers for an upper extremity, `12–15` for lower; fiberglass sets faster and is lighter. Pad bony prominences `2–3` layers, no wrinkles. Wrap distal to proximal and leave fingers and toes exposed.

## CMS / PMS checks

- **Circulation:** distal pulse, capillary refill under `2 s`, color, temperature
- **Motor:** wiggle fingers or toes, then move against resistance
- **Sensation:** light touch distal to the injury, compare sides

Check and document **before and after** every splint, and again after any transport or reduction.

> **Trap:** A pulse that was there before splinting and gone after is a splint that comes off *now*, not a finding to chart and move on from.

## Crutch and cane fitting

- Axillary pad `2–3` finger widths (about `1.5–2 in` / `4–5 cm`) below the armpit — weight goes on the hands, never the armpit
- Handgrip at the wrist crease with the arm hanging; elbow bent `20–30` degrees
- Tips rest `6 in` (`15 cm`) in front and `2 in` (`5 cm`) to the side of the foot
- Stairs: **up with the good leg first, down with the bad leg and crutches first**
- Cane goes in the hand **opposite** the injured leg; top at the wrist crease, elbow `15–30` degrees

## Wound irrigation

| Item | Number |
|---|---|
| Pressure | `5–8 psi` (some texts `7–15 psi`) |
| How to get it | `35–60 mL` syringe with an `18–19 G` angiocath or a splash shield |
| Volume | `50–100 mL` per cm of wound length; at least `250–500 mL` for a simple laceration, `1–2 L` if contaminated |
| Solution | Normal saline or potable tap water — outcomes are equivalent |

## Local anesthetic maximums

| Agent | Max dose | Onset / duration |
|---|---|---|
| Lidocaine `1%` plain | `4.5 mg/kg`, max `300 mg` (`30 mL` of `1%`) | `2–5 min` / `30–120 min` |
| Lidocaine with epinephrine | `7 mg/kg`, max `500 mg` (`50 mL` of `1%`) | `2–5 min` / `2–6 h` |
| Bupivacaine plain | `2.5 mg/kg`, max `175 mg` | `5–10 min` / `4–8 h` |
| Bupivacaine with epinephrine | `3 mg/kg`, max `225 mg` | `5–10 min` / `4–8 h` |

A `1%` solution is `10 mg/mL`. Buffer with sodium bicarbonate `1:10` to cut the sting. Epinephrine-containing solutions are now considered safe in digits in routine practice, but many departments still restrict it — follow protocol.

## Suture size and removal

| Location | Size | Remove at |
|---|---|---|
| Face, eyelid | `6-0` (`5-0`) | `3–5 d` |
| Neck | `5-0` | `4–6 d` |
| Scalp | `3-0` or `4-0` | `7–10 d` |
| Arm, hand | `4-0` or `5-0` | `7–10 d` |
| Trunk, chest, abdomen | `3-0` or `4-0` | `7–12 d` |
| Back | `3-0` | `10–14 d` |
| Leg, foot, over a joint | `3-0` or `4-0` | `10–14 d` |
| Oral mucosa | `4-0` absorbable | Dissolves |

Bigger number means thinner thread. `6-0` is finer than `3-0`.

## Tetanus

| Wound | `3` or more prior doses | Fewer than `3` or unknown |
|---|---|---|
| Clean, minor | Td/Tdap only if the last dose was `10 y` ago or more | Give Td/Tdap. No TIG |
| All other wounds (dirty, puncture, crush, burn, frostbite, missile, avulsion) | Td/Tdap if the last dose was `5 y` ago or more | Give Td/Tdap **and** tetanus immune globulin `250 units` IM at a separate site |

Tdap is preferred over Td for anyone who has never had a Tdap.

## Dressing by wound

| Wound | Dressing |
|---|---|
| Clean sutured laceration | Nonadherent contact layer plus dry gauze |
| Abrasion | Nonadherent or petrolatum gauze; hydrocolloid for shallow clean areas |
| Skin tear | Silicone or nonadherent; never tape fragile skin |
| Superficial partial-thickness burn | Nonadherent plus bulky dry gauze. No ice, no butter |
| Heavily draining | Alginate or foam |
| Necrotic or sloughy | Hydrogel for autolytic debridement |
| Infected | Non-occlusive, changed daily |
| Actively bleeding | Direct pressure, hemostatic gauze, tourniquet if extremity and uncontrolled |
| Evisceration | Moist sterile saline gauze, then an occlusive layer over it. Never push organs back |
| Open chest wound | Vented chest seal |
| Amputated part | Moist sterile gauze, sealed bag, bag placed on ice water — never directly on ice |

## Urinary catheters

- French size is the **circumference in mm**; `1 Fr` is about `1/3 mm` of diameter. Bigger number, bigger tube.
- Adult female `14 Fr`; adult male `14–16 Fr`; `16 Fr` is the default.
- Gross hematuria with clots: `20–24 Fr` three-way for continuous bladder irrigation.
- Pediatrics `6–10 Fr`; infants `5–6 Fr`.
- Coudé tip for a man with an enlarged prostate — point the curve up.
- **Balloon:** inflate with sterile water to the volume printed on the inflation port, usually `10 mL`; `30 mL` balloons exist for post-op and irrigation. Never inflate before urine returns.
- Insertion depth: female `2–3 in` (`5–7.5 cm`); male `7–9 in` (`17–22 cm`). Once urine flows, advance another `1–2 in` before inflating.
- Straight (in-and-out) catheters are the same sizes without a balloon, used for a single drain or a sterile specimen.

## Bladder scan and eye irrigation

| Finding | Action |
|---|---|
| Post-void residual under `50 mL` | Normal |
| `50–100 mL` | Borderline, recheck |
| Over `150 mL` | Abnormal retention |
| `300–400 mL` or more | Catheterize per protocol |
| Over `500 mL` | Significant retention, drain |

Morgan lens or eye irrigation: anesthetize first (proparacaine), irrigate with `1–2 L` per eye over at least `15–30 min`, and keep going until the pH measured in the lower fornix is `7.0–7.4`. Recheck the pH `5–10 min` after stopping — alkali burns rebound and often need several liters more.
